(Original data from the Statistical Abstract of the US, 1992)

solution.p: The integral \int_0^{50}{f(t)dt} represents the total emissions of nitrogen oxides, in millions of metric tons, during the period 1940 to 1990.

We estimate the integral using left- and right-hand sums: \mbox{Left sum} = (7)(10) + (9)(10) + (12.8)(10) + (18.8)(10) + (21)(10) = 686, and \mbox{Right sum} = (9)(10) + (12.8)(10) + (18.8)(10) + (21)(10) + (19.4)(10) = 810. We can then average the left- and right-hand sums to find the best estimate of the integral: \int_0^{50}{f(t)dt} \approx {{686 + 810} \over 2} = 748 \mbox{ million metric tons.} Between 1940 and 1990, about 748 million metric tons of nitrogen oxides were emitted.

statement.p: (a) What is the exact value of \int_{0}^{3}\,e^x\,dx?
Find LEFT(2), RIGHT(2), TRAP(2), MID(2), and SIMP(4); compute the error for each.
Repeat part (b) with n=4 (instead of n=2).

static.solution:
(a) \int_{0}^{3}\,e^x\,dx = e^x\bigg|_{0}^{3} = e^3 - e^0 \approx 19.0855\ldots
(b) Computing the sums directly, since \Delta x=1.5, we have
LEFT(2) = 1.5\cdot e^0 + 1.5\cdot e^{1.5} \approx 8.2225
RIGHT(2) = 1.5\cdot e^{1.5} + 1.5\cdot e^{3} \approx 36.8509
TRAP(2) = \frac 1 2 ( 8.2225 + 36.8509 ) \approx 22.5367
MID(2) = 1.5\cdot e^{0.75} + 1.5\cdot e^{3\cdot 0.75} \approx 17.4072
and SIMP(4) = (2 MID(2) + TRAP(2))/3 \approx 19.117.
And the errors are just the actual value minus the approximate values, or
error(LEFT(2)) = 10.863; error(RIGHT(2)) = -17.7654; error(TRAP(2)) = -3.4512; error(MID(2)) = 1.6784; and error(SIMP(4)) = -0.0315.
(c) Similarly, since \Delta x = 0.375, we have
LEFT(4) = 12.8149; error = 6.2707
RIGHT(4) = 27.129; error = -8.0435
TRAP(4) = 19.9719; error = -0.8864
MID(4) = 18.6455; error = 0.44
SIMP(8) = 19.0876; error = -0.0021.
(d) For LEFT and RIGHT, we expect the error to go down by 1/2, and this is very roughly what we see. For MID and TRAP, we expect the error to go down by 1/4, and this is approximately what we see. For SIMP, we expect the error to go down by 1/16, again as observed.

static.solution:
Thus we get different solution behaviors for the initial conditions P(0) = 1, P(0) > 1, and 0 \lt P(0) \lt 1. The initial condition P(0) = 0 gives the zero solution, which is an equilibrium and has the same behavior as the initial condition P(0) = 1. Note that we can also say that the behavior for initial conditions 0 \lt P(0) \lt 0.5 is different from that for initial conditions 0.5 \le P(0) \lt 1, because the former will be sigmoidal while the latter are strictly exponential.
From the solutions graphed above, or by looking at the slope field, we can see that the equilibrium solution P = 1 is stable. The other equilibrium solution, P = 0 is unstable.
Also by looking at the solution curves, we can see that P is increasing when 0 \lt P \lt 1 and decreasing when P > 1. In the long run, we're most likely to start with a non-zero population and thus P\to 1. The solution curves with initial populations of less than P= 0.5 have inflection points at P=0.5. (This will be demonstrated algebraically below.) At the inflection point, the population is growing fastest.
A graph of dP/dt against P is shown below.
Since \frac{dP}{dt}=5 P - 5 P^2 = 5 P(1 - P), the graph of \frac{dP}{dt} against P is a parabola, opening downward with P intercepts at 0 and 1. The quantity \frac{dP}{dt} is positive for 0 \lt P \lt 1, negative for P > 1 (and P \lt 0). The quantity \frac{dP}{dt} is 0 at P=0 and P=, and maximum at P=0.5. The fact that \frac{dP}{dt} =0 at P=0 and P=1 tells us that these are equilibria. Further, since \frac{dP}{dt}> 0 for 0 \lt P \lt 1, we see that solution curves starting here will increase toward P=1.
If the population starts at a value P\lt 0.5, it increases at an increasing rate up to P=0.5. After this, P continues to increase, but at a decreasing rate. The fact that \frac{dP}{dt} has a maximum at P=0.5 tells us that there is a point of inflection when P=0.5. Similarly, since \frac{dP}{dt} \lt 0 for P > 1, solution curves starting with P > 1 will decrease to P = 1. Thus, P=1 is a stable equilibrium.

statement.p: The total number of people infected with a virus often grows like a logistic curve. Suppose that 10 people originally have the virus, and that in the early stages of the virus (with time, t, measured in weeks), the number of people infected is increasing exponentially with k=2. It is estimated that, in the long run, approximately 6500 people become infected.
(a) Use this information to find a logistic function to model this situation.

(b) Sketch a graph of your answer to part (a). Use your graph to estimate the length of time until the rate at which people are becoming infected starts to decrease. What is the vertical coordinate at this point?
vertical coordinate =

static.solution:
(a) We know that a logistic curve can be modeled by the function P=\frac{L}{1+Ce^{-kt}} where C=(L-P_0)/P_0 and P is the number of people infected by the virus at a particular time t. We know that L is the limiting value, or the maximal number of people infected with the virus, so in our case L=6500. We are also told that initially there are only 10 people infected with the virus so that we get P_0=10. Thus we have C = \frac{L-P_0}{P_0} = \frac{6500-10}{10} = 649. We are also told that in the early stages of the virus, infection grows exponentially with k=2. Thus we get that the logistic function for people infected is P=\frac{6500}{1+649 e^{-2 t}}.
(b) Graphing this solution, we see
Looking at the graph we see that the the point at which the rate changes from increasing to decreasing, the inflection point, occurs at roughly t=3.25 giving a value of P=3375. Thus after roughly 3375 people have been infected, the rate of infection starts dropping.

statement.p: Any population, P, for which we can ignore immigration, satisfies \frac{dP}{dt} =\hbox{Birth rate} - \hbox{Death rate}.

For organisms which need a partner for reproduction but rely on a chance encounter for meeting a mate, the birth rate is proportional to the square of the population. Thus, the population of such a type of organism satisfies a differential equation of the form \frac{dP}{dt} = a P^2 - b P\quad\hbox{with } a,\,b>0. This problem investigates the solutions to such an equation.

If P(0) = b/a, what happens to P in the long run?
If P(0) \lt b/a, what happens to P in the long run?

static.solution:
(a) A graph of dP/dt vs P is shown below.
Thus, dP/dt is negative when 0 \lt P \lt b/a and positive when b/a \lt P \lt \infty (we ignore P \lt 0, because this doesn't make sense for a population).
(b)
We can see from the graph above that P is a decreasing function when P\lt \frac{b}{a}. Similarly, when P>\frac{b}{a}, the sign of dP/dt is positive, so P is an increasing function. Thus solution curves starting above \frac{b}{a} are increasing, and those starting below \frac{b}{a} are decreasing.
We can also see that for P>\frac{b}{a}, the slope, \frac{dP}{dt}, increases with P, so the graph of P against t is concave up. For 0\lt P\lt \frac{b}{a}, the value of P decreases with time. As P decreases, the slope \frac{dP}{dt} decreases for \frac{b}{2a}\lt P\lt \frac{b}{a}, and increases toward 0 for 0\lt P\lt \frac{b}{2a}. Thus solution curves starting just below the threshold value of \frac{b}{a} are concave down for \frac{b}{2a}\lt P\lt \frac{b}{a} and concave up and asymptotic to the t-axis for 0\lt P\lt \frac{b}{2a}. Thus, solution curves are similar to those shown in the graph below
P=\frac{b}{a} is called the threshold population because for populations greater than \frac{b}{a}, the population will increase without bound. For populations less than \frac{b}{a}, the population will go to zero, i.e. to extinction. The value \frac{b}{a} is an unstable equilibrium, and P=0 is a stable equilibrium.

static.solution:
T_2(x) is the second degree Taylor polynomial for f(x) about x=0, T_2(0)=f(0), which says c_0=f(0). Since \frac{d}{dx}T_2(x) \big|_{x=0} = f'(0), c_1=f'(0); and since \frac{d^2}{dx^2} T_2(x) \big|_{x=0} = f''(0), 2c_2=f''(0). In other words, c_0 is the y-intercept of f(x), c_1 is the slope of the tangent line to f(x) at x=0 and c_2 tells us the concavity of f(x) near x=0.
Thus c_0 > 0; c_1 \lt 0; and c_2 > 0

statement.p: Calculate the Taylor polynomials T_2(x) and T_3(x) centered at x = \pi for f(x) = \sin\mathopen{}\left(x\right).

static.solution:
\begin{array}{lcll} T(x) \amp = \amp \amp f(a) \cr\cr \amp \amp + \amp \frac{f'(a)}{1!} (x-a) \cr \cr \amp \amp + \amp \frac{f''(a)}{2!} (x-a)^2 \cr \cr \amp \amp + \amp \ldots \cr \cr \amp \amp + \amp \frac{f^n(a)}{n!} (x-a)^n \end{array}
So, in this case, f(x) = \sin\mathopen{}\left(x\right) and
T_2(x) = A + B(x-\pi ) + C(x-\pi )^2
where
A=f(\pi )=0=0
B=f'(\pi )=-1=-1
C=\frac{f''(\pi )}{2!}=0=0
Thus,
T_2(x) = 0 - 1 (x - \pi ) + 0 (x - \pi )^2
or
T_2(x) = -\left(x-\pi \right)
Similarly,
T_3(x) = D + E(x-\pi ) + F(x-\pi )^2 + G(x-\pi )^3
where
D=f(\pi )=0 = 0
E=f'(\pi )=-1 =-1
F=\frac{f''(\pi )}{2!}=0 =0
G=\frac{f'''(\pi )}{3!}=\frac{1}{6}=0.166666666666667
Thus, T_3(x) = 0 - 1 (x - \pi ) + 0 (x - \pi )^2 + \frac{1}{6} (x - \pi )^3
or
T_3(x) = 0.166667\mathopen{}\left(x-\pi \right)^{3}-\left(x-\pi \right)

solution.p: We use the ratio test: \left|{a_{n+1} \over {a_n}}\right| = \left|{{(n+1)^4 x^{2(n+1)}} \over {2^{2(n+1)}}} \cdot {{2^{2 n}} \over {n^4 x^{2 n}}}\right| = \left({{n+1} \over n}\right)^2 \cdot {{x^2} \over 4}. Since {{(n+1)}/ n} \rightarrow 1 as n \rightarrow \infty, we have \lim_{n\to\infty} \left|{{a_{n+1}} \over {a_n}}\right|={{x^2}\over 4}. We have {{x^2}/ 4} \lt 1 when |x| \lt 2. solution.p: The n^{th} degree approximation of f(1.09) about x=1 is given by:
